source.title: Self-conditioned Embedding Diffusion for Text Generation
source.authors: Robin Strudel; Corentin Tallec; Florent Altché; Yilun Du; Y. Ganin; Arthur Mensch; Will Grathwohl; N. Savinov; S. Dieleman; L. Sifre; R. Leblond

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites Hoffmann et al.'s compute-optimal scaling laws and says its AR baselines follow them, but does not test the claimed power laws or compute-optimal allocation. Its own two-size comparison reports generated-sample quality, not held-out pretraining loss or a fitted scaling law.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a two-size SED comparison using AR NLL of generated samples and human preferences; these measures do not test any listed version. The reference to Hoffmann et al. is used to set up AR baselines, not reported as a result of this study. Other AR NLL and entropy results concern model design and sampling comparisons, not the claimed scaling laws.
record.test_reason: This paper proposes a text diffusion model (SED). It uses Hoffmann et al.'s compute-optimal laws only to configure its AR baselines. Its only size comparison is two SED models (135–150m vs 420m). That comparison is scored by the AR NLL of generated samples and by human preference. It reports no held-out pretraining loss curve, power-law fit, extrapolation, allocation sweep, shape study or downstream-task scaling, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors say SED rivals AR models of similar size on the NLL/entropy trade-off. Humans still slightly prefer AR models, and SED-L is roughly on par with AR-S. Scaling SED-S to SED-L improves sample quality. They add that larger scaling and more tuning are needed.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce the original scaling-law measurement. It uses Hoffmann et al.'s scaling laws to configure AR comparison baselines and evaluates a two-size diffusion-model comparison with generated-sample metrics.

fits_no_version.finding: SED-L (420m) gives generated samples with lower AR NLL than SED-S: 3.68 vs 4.20 at sequence length 256.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger continuous text diffusion models produce higher-quality samples as judged by a strong AR model.

fits_no_version.finding: Human raters preferred SED-L over SED-S on the conditional task 63.4% ± 4.3% of the time.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Human raters prefer samples from the larger of two text diffusion models.

record.problems: The size comparison includes only two SED models, and its AR NLL is for generated samples rather than held-out pretraining loss. No power-law fit, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation test, or uncertainty estimate for the AR NLL comparison is reported.

untested.parts: No held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No small-run fit used to predict larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation study. Hoffmann laws are only applied to set AR baselines.
No comparison of depth or width at a fixed parameter count.
Text diffusion is a different training regime, but with two sizes and sample metrics no power-law form is tested.
No downstream-task performance versus scale or loss.
No analysis of fitting choices or of curve bending.

record.verdict_notes: This is a model-proposal paper with no scaling-law result. The evaluator AR model is described as 70B parameters 'trained on 1.4B tokens', which is likely a typo for 1.4T. None of the ablations (embedding dimension, span count, self-conditioning) bear on V4, which concerns transformer shape at fixed parameter count.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run power-law fit or prediction of much larger runs is reported.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or fitted parameter/token growth trends are reported.
The paper does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at a fixed parameter count.
The paper studies text diffusion but does not test whether the same power-law form holds in this or other training regimes.
The paper measures generated-sample quality, not downstream-task performance or its predictability from pretraining loss.
No analysis of fit dependence, competing exponents, or departures from a single power law is reported.

rows.subject: SED-L
rows.operation_detail: Compared generated-sample AR NLL with SED-S in a two-size model comparison.
rows.note: The authors report this as an improvement in sample quality when scaling SED-S to SED-L. It is not held-out pretraining loss.
rows.check: The measure is the 70B AR model's NLL of SED's generated samples, not held-out loss, and there are only two sizes, so no power law can be read. SED-S size is inconsistent in the paper: 135m in Section 4.1, 150m in Section 4.4. The row's condition uses 150m; this should be noted.

rows.subject: SED-L
rows.operation_detail: Reported human preference for the larger SED model in the size comparison.
rows.note: The text describes the larger model's human preference score as 63%; Table 4 gives 63.4% ± 4.3%.
rows.check: Human preference of SED-L over SED-S on the conditional (suffix in-filling) task is a sample-quality judgement, not loss or a downstream-task metric. The 63.4% ± 4.3% value matches Table 4.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
